newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan officials concerned about weak yen, stocks.
newsitem.headline: Japan officials concerned about weak yen, stocks.

text.p: The sharp falls in the Japanese yen and Tokyo's stock market may undermine an economic recovery that would be in good shape otherwise, top government officials said on Wednesday.

Tokyo shares have plunged some 14 percent since early December and the Japanese yen is at its weakest level against the dollar in nearly four years because of concerns about the health of the economy.

"The pace of recent developments in the currency markets has been rather fast and we will continue to watch the effects on the economy closely," Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita told a news conference.
He also said the recent fall in stock prices was one reason for continued doubts about the economy on the part of corporate leaders.

On Wednesday, the Tokyo market's key barometer, the 225-share Nikkei average, recovered some of the ground it has lost so far this year. It closed up 3.78 percent at 18,013.88 after a drop of some 10 percent since the start of the year.
The yen, meanwhile, fell to a 46-month low of 118.75 against the dollar on the back of persistent worries among market players about the health of Japanese banks.
"An excessively weak yen or strong yen is not favourable for the Japanese economy. Currency stability is important," Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said in parliament.

Matsushita said the central bank would maintain its its easy credit stance to ensure that a favourable economic cycle of production leading an increase in incomes and thus spending strengthened further.
Japan's economy has been recovering slowly since the start of last year after emerging from four years of negligible growth.
However, pessimism has grown rapidly as Hashimoto in December proposed a tight budget for the coming fiscal year starting on April 1 in order to get Japan's big budget deficit under control.
"Our view has been that the economy is continuing to recover gradually, and at the moment the strength of the recovery is becoming firmer," Matsushita said.
He said that the fall in stock prices could hurt the profits of financial institutions.
"We cannot ignore the effect on the bad loans problems of individual institutions and their earnings results," he said.
Weak share prices make it harder for companies to raise capital, either from the market or from banks, which have made increasingly cautious by their own battered balance sheets.
